source_text: Ceterum et si esse eum possemus confiteri, sine causa esse eum deberemus argumentari. sine causa enim esset qui rem non haberet, quia res omnis causa est, ut sit aliquis, cuius res sit. porro in quantum nihil oportet esse sine causa, [id est sine re] quia si sine causa sit, proinde est atque si non sit. [non habens rei causam rem ipsam] in tantum deum dignius credam non esse quam esse sine causa. sine causa est enim qui rem non habendo non habet causam. deus autem sine causa, id est sine re, esse non debet. ita quotiens ostendo eum sine causa esse, tamquam sit, hoc constituo, non esse illum, quia si fuisset, omnino sine causa non fuisset. sic et ipsam fidem dico illum sine causa ab homine captare. aliter solito deum credere ex operum auctoritate formatum. quia nihil tale prospexit, per quod homo deum didicit. nam etsi credunt plerique in illum, non statim ratione credunt. non habentes dei pignus, opera eius deo digna. itaque hoc nomine cessationis et defectionis operum et impudentiae et malignitatis adfinis est: impudentiae, qua fidem non debitam sibi captat, cui praestruendae nihil prospexit. malignitatis. qua plures incredulitatis reos fecit, nihil fidei procurando.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover, even if we could confess that He exists, we would have to argue that He exists without cause. For He would be without cause who does not have a thing, because every thing is a cause, so that there may be someone whose thing it is. Furthermore, insofar as nothing ought to be without cause, that is, without a thing, because if it is without cause, it is just as if it does not exist. Not having the cause of a thing, it does not have the thing itself. To this extent, I consider it more worthy of God not to exist than to exist without cause. For He is without cause who, not having a thing, does not have a cause. But God ought not to exist without cause, that is, without a thing. Thus, whenever I show that He exists without cause, as if He exists, I establish that He does not exist, because if He had existed, He would not have existed without cause at all. So also I say that faith captures Him without cause from man. Otherwise, it is customary to believe in God, formed from the authority of works. Because He did not foresee anything of this kind, through which man learned about God. For even if many believe in Him, they do not believe immediately by reason. Not having God's pledge, His works worthy of God. And so, by this name of cessation and defection of works and impudence and malice, He is related to impudence, by which He captures faith not owed to Him, for whom He did not foresee anything to be laid out. Of malice, by which He made many guilty of unbelief, procuring nothing for faith.

choices.why: accurate translation of the sense of debt

pass_b_english: Even if we could admit He exists, we would still have to argue that He exists without cause. Anything without cause lacks a thing, because every thing is a cause — it exists so that there is someone whose thing it is. Since nothing ought to be without cause, that is, without a thing — for if it is without cause, it might as well not exist — lacking the cause of a thing means lacking the thing itself. To that extent, I judge it more fitting for God not to exist than to exist without cause. He is without cause who, by not having a thing, has no cause. But God ought not to exist without cause, that is, without a thing. So every time I demonstrate that He exists without cause, as if He exists, I prove He does not exist — because if He had existed, He would not have existed without cause at all.

Thus I also say that faith seizes Him without cause from man. Normally one believes in God shaped by the authority of works. But He foresaw nothing of the kind through which man might learn of God. Even though many believe in Him, they do not believe by reason straightaway. They lack God's pledge, His works worthy of God. And so, under this name of cessation and defection of works, of impudence and malice, He is kin to impudence — which snatches faith not owed to Him, for whom He foresaw nothing to be laid out — and to malice — which made many guilty of unbelief, securing nothing for faith.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the complex philosophical argument regarding 'causa' and 'res' in Tertullian's Latin. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin. The distinction between 'sine causa' (without cause) and 'sine re' (without a thing) is maintained. The translation of 'impudentiae... et malignitatis adfinis est' as being 'related to' or 'kin to' these qualities is accurate.
source: 'sine causa esse eum deberemus argumentari', english: 'we would have to argue that He exists without cause'
